title: ISC U2·W1 — SOC Engagements: SOC 1, SOC 2 & SOC 3 (CPA Discipline)
lessonHtml:
Cold open — assurance over someone else's controls

When Meridian Building Group outsources payroll, hosting, or an application, the controls over its data sit at the service organization — yet MBG remains accountable. System and Organization Controls (SOC) reports are how a service organization gives its customers assurance over those controls, examined by an independent service auditor. AUD Unit 3 met SOC reports from the user auditor's side; this ISC unit examines them from the inside — the types of SOC engagement, the parties, and what each report does and does not provide.

Why SOC reports exist

Outsourcing transfers operation of a control to a third party but not responsibility for it. A user organization cannot practically send its auditors into every vendor, and the vendor cannot host dozens of separate customer audits. The SOC report solves this: the service organization engages one service auditor to examine its controls and issue a report its many customers (and their auditors) can rely on. It is the efficient, standardized answer to "can I trust the controls at my vendor?" — the assurance backbone of a cloud-and-outsourcing economy.

SOC 1 — controls relevant to financial reporting

A SOC 1 report addresses controls at a service organization that are relevant to user entities' internal control over financial reporting (ICFR) — for example, a payroll processor's controls over calculating and recording pay. It is performed under the attestation standards (AT-C 320), is restricted in use to the service organization, its user entities, and their auditors, and is precisely the report a user auditor obtains to rely on the service organization's controls (AUD Unit 3). SOC 1 answers the financial-statement-audit question: do the vendor's controls support the numbers that flow into my books?

SOC 2 — the trust services criteria

A SOC 2 report addresses controls relevant to security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality, and privacy — the Trust Services Criteria (covered in depth next week) — rather than financial reporting. It serves a broader set of stakeholders (customers, regulators, business partners) who care about how a vendor protects systems and data, and like SOC 1 it is restricted in use to parties with sufficient knowledge of the system. SOC 2 is the report a company requests when evaluating a cloud provider's security posture — the dominant report in vendor-risk management.

SOC 3 — general use

A SOC 3 report covers the same Trust Services Criteria as SOC 2 but is a general-use, summary report: it provides the auditor's opinion and a short description without the detailed description of controls and tests that make SOC 2 restricted. Because it omits the sensitive detail, a SOC 3 can be freely distributed — posted on a website or shared in marketing as a seal of assurance. The trade-off is depth: SOC 3 tells the public "an independent auditor examined our security controls," while SOC 2 gives a knowledgeable user the evidence to evaluate them.

Type 1 versus Type 2

SOC 1 and SOC 2 each come in two types, the same distinction as in AUD Unit 3. A Type 1 report opines on whether the controls are suitably designed at a point in time. A Type 2 report goes further, opining on whether the controls were operating effectively over a period (typically six to twelve months) and including the auditor's tests of controls and the results. Only a Type 2 report supports a user's reliance on the operating effectiveness of the controls — a Type 1 confirms the design but not that the controls actually worked.

The parties to a SOC engagement

A SOC engagement involves defined roles. The service organization operates the system and makes a written assertion about its controls. The service auditor (an independent CPA firm) examines and reports. The user entity is the customer relying on the report, and its user auditor may use the report in the financial-statement audit. When the service organization itself relies on a subservice organization (e.g., a SaaS vendor hosted on a cloud provider), the report uses either the carve-out method (excluding the subservice org's controls, noting them) or the inclusive method (covering them) — a distinction users must understand to know what the report actually covers.

Complementary user-entity controls

A SOC report almost always assumes the user organization performs certain controls itself — the complementary user-entity controls (CUECs). For example, a payroll provider's controls work only if the user reviews and approves the payroll register and restricts who can submit changes. The report lists these CUECs, and the user's reliance on the service org's controls is conditional on performing them. A user that reads a clean SOC report but ignores the CUECs has a false sense of security — the assurance is a shared responsibility, not a transfer of it.

What a SOC report contains, and the SOC family

A SOC report follows a consistent structure worth knowing. It opens with the service auditor's opinion (unqualified/clean, or qualified by identified control exceptions), followed by management's written assertion about the system and the suitability of its controls, and a description of the system — its boundaries, infrastructure, software, people, data, and procedures. A Type 2 report then adds the service auditor's tests of controls and the results, the detailed evidence a knowledgeable user reads to judge operating effectiveness and the complementary user-entity controls. Beyond the SOC 1/2/3 trio, the AICPA also offers a SOC for Cybersecurity (an entity-wide cyber-risk-management examination, general use) and SOC for Supply Chain — the same examination model extended to new subject matter as assurance needs expand. Reading any SOC report therefore begins with checking its type (1 vs 2), its category coverage, and its opinion before placing reliance on it.

CMA bridge

When MBG moves payroll or job-cost hosting to a vendor, the CFO should obtain and read the vendor's SOC 1 Type 2 (for the financial-reporting controls) or SOC 2 (for security) — and confirm MBG performs the complementary user-entity controls. This is the practical vendor-risk discipline behind the outsourcing decisions a finance function makes constantly.

Practice and recap

  1. Match the report to the need: SOC 1 = controls over user ICFR (financial reporting); SOC 2 = Trust Services Criteria (security/availability/processing integrity/confidentiality/privacy); SOC 3 = general-use summary of SOC 2 subject matter.
  2. Distinguish Type 1 (design at a point in time) from Type 2 (operating effectiveness over a period, with tests + results); only Type 2 supports reliance on operating effectiveness.
  3. Identify the parties: service organization (assertion), service auditor, user entity, user auditor, subservice organization (carve-out vs inclusive).
  4. Recognize complementary user-entity controls (CUECs) — reliance is conditional on the user performing them.

Recap: SOC reports give a service organization's customers independent assurance over its controls — SOC 1 covers controls relevant to user financial reporting (restricted use), SOC 2 covers the Trust Services Criteria for broader stakeholders (restricted use), and SOC 3 is a general-use summary of the SOC 2 subject matter; SOC 1 and SOC 2 come as Type 1 (design at a point) or Type 2 (operating effectiveness over a period, with tests), and only Type 2 supports reliance on effectiveness; the engagement involves the service organization, service auditor, user entity and its auditor, and any subservice organization (carve-out or inclusive), with complementary user-entity controls making the assurance a shared responsibility.

flashcards.back: SOC 1: controls relevant to user ICFR (financial reporting). SOC 2: Trust Services Criteria (security/availability/processing integrity/confidentiality/privacy). SOC 3: general-use summary of SOC 2 subject matter (no detail).

flashcards.front: SOC 1/2 restricted vs SOC 3 general use
flashcards.back: SOC 1 and SOC 2 are restricted to parties with knowledge of the system; SOC 3 omits the detailed description/tests so it can be distributed freely (a public seal).
Type 1: suitability of design at a point in time. Type 2: operating effectiveness over a period (6–12 mo) + tests and results. Only Type 2 supports reliance on operating effectiveness.
Security, Availability, Processing Integrity, Confidentiality, Privacy. Security is the baseline 'common criteria'; the others are added as relevant.
Service organization (makes the assertion), service auditor (examines/reports), user entity (relies), user auditor (may use it in the audit), subservice organization (vendor's vendor).
For a subservice organization: carve-out excludes its controls from the report (notes them); inclusive covers them. Affects what the report actually assures.
Controls the SOC report assumes the USER performs (e.g., review the payroll register). Reliance on the service org's controls is conditional on performing the CUECs.

flashcards.front: Which SOC for a cloud vendor's security?
flashcards.back: SOC 2 (Trust Services Criteria), typically Type 2, for vendor-risk evaluation; SOC 1 is for controls affecting the user's financial reporting.

questions.q: A SOC 1 report addresses controls relevant to:
choices: User entities' internal control over financial reporting
questions.explain: SOC 1 covers controls at a service organization relevant to user ICFR.

questions.q: Which report uses the Trust Services Criteria and is restricted to knowledgeable users?
questions.explain: SOC 2 reports on the Trust Services Criteria and is restricted; SOC 3 is the general-use summary.

questions.q: A SOC 3 report differs from SOC 2 in that it is:
choices: General use, without the detailed description and tests
questions.explain: SOC 3 covers the same subject matter but omits the detail, so it can be freely distributed.

questions.q: Only which type of SOC report supports reliance on operating effectiveness?
questions.explain: Type 2 tests operating effectiveness over a period; Type 1 only opines on design at a point in time.

questions.q: The party that makes the written assertion about its controls is the:
questions.explain: The service organization asserts about its controls; the service auditor examines and reports.

questions.q: Excluding a subservice organization's controls from the report (noting them) is the:
questions.explain: Carve-out excludes the subservice org's controls; the inclusive method covers them.

choices: Controls the user organization must perform for the service org's controls to be effective
questions.explain: A SOC report assumes the user performs certain controls; reliance is conditional on them.
